common_name: Singapore Pink Bougainvillea (Compact Lavender-Pink Bougainvillea, Singapore Beauty)

planting.note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Singapore Pink is a thornless-looking, dense-branching selection well suited to hedges and screens.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean soil in full sun. Singapore Pink was developed in Singapore in the mid-1990s and is distinguished from most bougainvillea by its bushy, self-branching habit, larger leaves, and comparatively few, short thorns, which make it far easier to handle and shear than thorny classics like Barbara Karst. It produces continuous clusters of large, bright lavender-pink bracts and tolerates salt spray, heat, and poor sandy soil better than many cultivars, making it a dependable coastal hedge, screen, or trellis plant. Avoid overwatering and excess nitrogen, both of which favor leafy growth over bract production.

common_name: Mary Palmer Bougainvillea (Bicolor White-and-Pink Bracted Bougainvillea)

planting.note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained, lean soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis, arbor, or fence able to support a vigorous climbing vine.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean soil in full sun with a strong support for its vigorous climbing growth. Mary Palmer's defining trait is that a single plant produces both pure white and pink bract clusters at the same time, an unusual genetic bract-color break rather than the age-related color shift seen in cultivars like Rosenka or the leaf variegation seen in Raspberry Ice, whose foliage stays plain green throughout. This parti-colored bract pattern has made it a long-standing collector's favorite and gave rise to the related sport 'Mary Palmer's Enchantment'. As with other vigorous spectabilis-type bougainvillea, keep water and fertilizer on the lean side to maximize bract production.

common_name: Juanita Hatten Bougainvillea (Fuchsia-Red Bougainvillea with Variegated New Growth)

planting.note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained, lean soil in full sun to light shade on a trellis, fence, or other support.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean soil in full sun to light shade with a sturdy support for its fast, vining growth. Juanita Hatten produces fiery fuchsia-red bracts around tiny creamy-white flowers in a display very similar in color and vigor to Barbara Karst, but is distinguished by new growth that emerges lightly variegated with pale green streaking before fading to solid dark green as the foliage matures. It tolerates hot, dry sites well and is a strong hummingbird and pollinator draw. Keep water and nitrogen fertilizer on the lean side, since lush feeding favors leafy growth at the expense of bracts.

common_name: Camarillo Fiesta Bougainvillea (Bicolor Hot Pink and Orange-Gold Bougainvillea)

planting.note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained, lean soil in full sun on a trellis, arbor, or fence able to support a vigorous climbing vine.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean soil in full sun with a strong support for its vigorous climbing habit. Camarillo Fiesta (registered as 'Monle') is one of the most dramatically bicolor bougainvillea cultivars available, bearing hot pink and burnished orange-gold bracts together within the same cluster rather than shifting from one tone to another with age like James Walker or Rosenka. The bold two-tone effect intensifies in strong heat and full sun. Keep water and fertilizer lean to encourage the heaviest, most colorful bract production.

common_name: Jamaica White Bougainvillea (Pure White with Pink Blush Bougainvillea)

planting.note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained, lean soil in full sun on a trellis, arbor, wall, or fence able to support a vigorous climbing vine.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean soil in full sun with a strong support for its vigorous climbing habit. Jamaica White stands apart from most bougainvillea in the dataset by producing clean white bracts with only a faint pink blush rather than the magenta, red, orange, or gold tones typical of the genus, giving it a softer, more luminous look against dark walls, pergolas, and courtyards. It is just as vigorous and heat-tolerant as red-bracted cultivars like Barbara Karst or San Diego Red, and blooms repeatedly through the warm season. Keep water and fertilizer lean, since excess of either promotes leafy growth over bract production.
sources: Devil Mountain Wholesale Nursery Plant Database

common_name: Diamantina Jade White Dipladenia (Compact Pure White Mandevilla)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed when soil and air are warm; in zone 9-10 plant March-May. Diamantina Jade White is a compact, mounding dipladenia-type mandevilla bred for containers and hanging baskets, not for climbing.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic potting mix; Diamantina Jade White forms a dense, self-branching mound rather than a climbing vine, so it needs no trellis and performs best in patio containers, hanging baskets, and window boxes. It is the rare pure white-flowered member of the compact Diamantina dipladenia series, contrasting with the coral-orange tones of Diamantina Coral Orange Sunrise already common in the trade, and its clean white trumpet flowers with a soft yellow throat pair easily with almost any companion planting. Regular light feeding sustains the heavy, continuous bloom, and the plant tolerates brief dry spells once established. Outside zone 10-11, grow as a warm-season container annual or overwinter indoors in bright light; wear gloves when handling cut stems, as the sap can irritate skin.

common_name: Diamantina Opal Yellow Dipladenia (Compact Yellow Mandevilla)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed when soil and air are warm; in zone 9-10 plant March-May. Diamantina Opal Yellow is a compact, mounding dipladenia-type mandevilla bred for containers and hanging baskets, not for climbing.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic potting mix; Diamantina Opal Yellow forms a dense, self-branching mound rather than a climbing vine, so it needs no trellis and performs best in patio containers, hanging baskets, and window boxes. Its soft golden-yellow trumpet flowers are an unusually rare color break for mandevilla and dipladenia, most of which bloom in shades of pink, red, or white, making it a standout accent among the compact Diamantina series. Regular light feeding sustains heavy, continuous bloom, and the plant tolerates brief dry spells once established. Outside zone 10-11, grow as a warm-season container annual or overwinter indoors in bright light; wear gloves when handling cut stems, as the sap can irritate skin.

common_name: Sun Parasol Garden Crimson Mandevilla (Compact Bedding Mandevilla)
scientific_name: Mandevilla x amabilis 'Sun Parasol Garden Crimson'

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed when soil and air are warm; in zone 9 plant March-May. Sun Parasol Garden Crimson is a naturally compact bedding-type mandevilla bred for mixed beds, borders, and containers without a trellis.

directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile soil. Sun Parasol Garden Crimson was bred as the first true bedding-plant mandevilla in the Sun Parasol line, with a naturally compact, mounding, minimally twining habit suited to 4-inch pot production, mixed borders, and patio containers rather than the tall trellis training needed by the original vining Sun Parasol Crimson. Its large, rich, saturated red flowers hold their color exceptionally well through summer heat and are produced in greater numbers than older mandevilla types. Feed lightly through the growing season and treat as a warm-season annual outside the tropics, since it has no cold tolerance.
sources: Suntory Flowers — Sun Parasol Garden Crimson variety page

common_name: Sun Parasol Garden White Mandevilla (Compact White Bedding Mandevilla)
scientific_name: Mandevilla x amabilis 'Sun Parasol Garden White'

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed when soil and air are warm; in zone 9 plant March-May. Sun Parasol Garden White is a naturally compact bedding-type mandevilla bred for mixed beds, borders, and containers without a trellis.

directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile soil. Sun Parasol Garden White is the first true white-flowered, compact bedding-type mandevilla in the Sun Parasol line, bred for naturally dwarf, mounding growth in 4-inch pots and landscape beds rather than climbing a trellis like the vining Sun Parasol cultivars. Its clean white trumpet flowers with a soft yellow throat are noted by the breeder for high disease resistance and easy garden performance compared to older mandevilla types. Feed lightly through the growing season and treat as a warm-season annual outside the tropics, since it has no cold tolerance.
sources: Suntory Flowers — Sun Parasol Garden White variety page

common_name: Hula Girl Hibiscus (Brilliant Yellow Tropical Hibiscus with Red Throat)

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings or plant container specimens after all frost risk has passed; Hula Girl bears large brilliant yellow flowers with a red throat on a vigorous, upright tropical hibiscus shrub.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Hula Girl is one of the few clear, solid-yellow tropical hibiscus cultivars, bearing large flowers with broad, overlapping yellow petals set off by a bright red throat and style column, a cleaner single-tone yellow than the blended orange-yellow-red veining seen in Fiesta. Blooms open nearly year-round in mild climates on a vigorous, upright shrub, with each individual flower lasting a single day before the next flush opens. Prune hard in early spring to encourage vigorous new growth and maximum bloom, and feed with a slow-release fertilizer every four to six weeks through the growing season.

common_name: Sunset Boulevard Hibiscus (Hollywood Hibiscus Series, Solid Deep Orange Tropical Hibiscus)

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings or plant container specimens after all frost risk has passed; Sunset Boulevard is a Hollywood Hibiscus series selection bred for compact habit and heavy repeat bloom.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Sunset Boulevard is part of the Proven Winners Hollywood Hibiscus breeding series and carries solid, saturated deep orange flowers rather than the multicolor orange-red-yellow blends seen in cultivars like Fiesta or Fifth of July already grown here. It was bred for a more compact, floriferous habit and more consistent repeat bloom than older heirloom tropical hibiscus. Prune hard in early spring to encourage vigorous new growth and maximum bloom, and feed with a slow-release fertilizer every four to six weeks through the growing season.
sources: Proven Winners Plant Database — Hollywood Hibiscus Sunset Boulevard

common_name: Disco Diva Hibiscus (Hollywood Hibiscus Series, Creamsicle Orange and Ruby Magenta Bicolor Tropical Hibiscus)

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings or plant container specimens after all frost risk has passed; Disco Diva is a Hollywood Hibiscus series selection bred for compact habit and heavy repeat bloom.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Disco Diva is part of the Proven Winners Hollywood Hibiscus breeding series and displays a bold, sharply defined bicolor bloom, with creamy orange outer petal zones giving way to a vivid ruby-magenta center, a much bolder two-tone contrast than the soft veining seen in Fiesta or the variegated foliage of Cooperi. It was bred for a compact habit and heavy repeat bloom compared to older heirloom tropical hibiscus. Prune hard in early spring to encourage vigorous new growth and maximum bloom, and feed with a slow-release fertilizer every four to six weeks through the growing season.
sources: Proven Winners Plant Database — Hollywood Hibiscus Disco Diva
